source_refs.note: Topic 21.3.1 (PDF 79-81); the SN2, SN1 and carbocation diagrams are redrawn. The book says primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes 'always' follow SN2 and SN1; the lesson says they react by these mechanisms.

blocks.text: Nucleophilic substitution involves two processes: the leaving group departs (the C-X bond breaks) and the nucleophile attacks (the C-Nu bond forms). If both happen together in one step, the mechanism is SN2. If they happen in two separate steps, bond breaking first and bond making second, the mechanism is SN1.

SN2 is a single-step mechanism. As soon as the nucleophile begins to attack the electrophilic carbon, the bond to the leaving group begins to break; bond formation and bond breaking go together. The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group. Because two molecules take part in this one (rate-determining) step, the reaction is bimolecular, and its rate depends on both concentrations: rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile], so it is second order (1 + 1 = 2).

blocks.alt: HO- with a lone pair attacks the delta+ carbon of bromomethane from the side opposite Br, while a second curly arrow moves the C-Br electrons onto Br. In brackets, the transition state HO...C...Br with both bonds dashed and a negative charge; then CH3OH + Br-. Below: rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile], second order.
blocks.caption: The SN2 mechanism (original diagram after the book's scheme).
blocks.long_description: The hydroxide ion approaches the carbon from the back, opposite the bromine. In the transition state the O-C bond is half made and the C-Br bond half broken, and the three hydrogens lie flat. Then bromide leaves and methanol forms; the other groups on the carbon are turned inside out like an umbrella.

blocks.text: Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2 when attacked by nucleophiles. This is for steric reasons: the carbon carries hydrogen atoms or only one alkyl group, so the nucleophile can reach and attack it easily.

SN1 has two steps. First the halogenoalkane ionises reversibly, in a solvent such as aqueous acetone or aqueous ethanol, giving a carbocation intermediate. Second, the nucleophile attacks the carbocation to give the product. The first step breaks a covalent bond, so it is slow; the second, the combination of oppositely charged ions, is fast. The slow first step is rate-determining and involves only one molecule, so the mechanism is unimolecular: rate = k[halogenoalkane], first order.

blocks.alt: Step 1 (slow): (CH3)3C-Br ionises to the tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+ and Br-. Step 2 (fast): (CH3)3C+ + OH- gives (CH3)3C-OH; rate = k[halogenoalkane], first order. Below: carbocation stability, tertiary (CH3)3C+ > secondary (CH3)2CH+ > primary CH3CH2+ > methyl CH3+.
blocks.caption: The SN1 mechanism and carbocation stability (original diagram after the book's schemes).
blocks.long_description: The rate depends only on how fast the halogenoalkane ionises, so it does not depend on the nucleophile's concentration. A carbocation is stabilised by alkyl groups, which push electron density towards the positive carbon (the +I inductive effect); the more alkyl groups, the more stable the carbocation and the more easily it forms.

blocks.text: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1 when attacked by nucleophiles. The main reason is that they form a stable tertiary carbocation; also, three bulky groups on the electrophilic carbon prevent the nucleophile from attacking from the back of the leaving group. A secondary halogenoalkane can react by either SN2 or SN1, depending on the solvent.
